newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition in censure debate.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition in censure debate.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led government was expected to weather a censure motion challenge on Tuesday amid rumblings of fresh discontent from the staunchly secular armed forces.
Deputies began debating whether to go ahead with a combined bid to topple the government by two leftist parties who say the coalition threatens Turkey's secularist system.

Defeat for the government on Tuesday, seen as an unlikely prospect, would be a major embarrassment for Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and would open the way for a full-blown censure motion within a week.

Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller, head of the conservative True Path Party (DYP) in the coalition, was confident her MPs would cast their ballots for the government despite unease at recent Islamist proposals by Erbakan's Welfare Party.
She refused to tell her party which way to vote.
"I do not regard it necessary for a decision to be taken in the group for a vote such as this. My confidence in my group is complete," Ciller told a party meeting.
The military is shaping up as the most serious obstacle to Erbakan, who became NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader last June in coalition with pro-Western conservative Ciller.

Analysts say the divided opposition appears incapable of mustering enough support from disgruntled government MPs to topple Erbakan despite increasing discontent about the direction the country is taking.

"Under today's conditions, it is not possible to bring down the government with this censure or a subsequent censure signed jointly by the whole of the opposition," said Bilal Cetin, columnist with the liberal daily Yeni Yuzyil.
The opposition would need to win a simple majority in the 550-seat assembly on Tuesday and then garner 276 votes in a later ballot.
Welfare has drawn fire from secular circles and upset the armed forces with recent Islam-based proposals, such as lifting a ban on female government workers wearing Islamic headscarves.
The Milliyet newspaper on Tuesday quoted navy chief Admiral Guven Erkaya as saying he had called on the military top brass to formally warn Erbakan against Islamist militancy.

"A decision must be taken to advise the government so that extreme religious movements do not put the future of the state in danger," Erkaya was quoted as telling a recent meeting of the National Security Council attended by Erbakan.
Commentators have predicted the generals will caution Erbakan at a meeting of the military-dominated council on Friday.

Erbakan said on Tuesday that the will of the Turkish people should be respected. "What is most important is the people not the state. The state only exists to serve the people," he told a Welfare meeting.
Anger at the Islamists by supporters of Turkey's secular system has not translated into effective action in parliament.

The opposition suffered a string of defeats last week when deputies voted not to impeach Ciller for alleged corruption during her three years as premier from 1993. Anti-government groups fell short by 19 votes in their best showing.
The coalition has already survived the defection of 17 MPs from Ciller's pro-market DYP. Shares in Istanbul closed 0.8 percent higher on Tuesday ahead of the vote.

The main opposition Motherland Party of Mesut Yilmaz has put forward another censure motion, expected to be heard next week. However, suggestions of a challenge to Yilmaz's leadership have undermined the strength of his opposition.
